In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, meaning: when they reach you and attend your assembly. The answer to the conditional is ﴿they say﴾. The majority read aymānahum with a fatḥah on the hamzah (aymānahum: "their oaths"); al-Hasan read it with a kasrah, and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Mujadilah.

This is the meaning of ṣadd in the sense of "turning away". It may also be from ṣudūd (turning away), meaning: they turned away from entering the way of Allah and establishing His commands. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, namely of hypocrisy and barring.

In sā'a (evil is) there is the sense of wonder. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the lying, the barring and the ugliness of their deeds. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿because they believed﴾, meaning: because they believed outwardly out of hypocrisy and then disbelieved inwardly; or they showed belief to the believers and showed disbelief to the disbelievers. This is explicit in the disbelief of the hypocrites. It was also said that the verse was revealed about a people who believed and then apostatised. The first is preferable, as the context indicates.

﴿So a seal was set upon their hearts﴾, meaning: it was sealed over them because of their disbelief.

The majority read fa-ṭubi'a ("so it was sealed") in the passive, with the prepositional phrase after it serving as the deputy of the subject. Zayd ibn Ali read it in the active, with the subject a pronoun referring to Allah, the Glorified. This is supported by the reading of al-A'mash: "fa-ṭaba'a Allāhu 'alā qulūbihim" ("so Allah sealed their hearts"). ﴿So they do not understand﴾ what is in it of their welfare and guidance, which is faith.

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you﴾, meaning: their forms and appearances. The sense is that they have bodies which please whoever sees them, because of their freshness and splendour. ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, so you deem their words true and sincere, because of their eloquence and fluency of tongue. Abdullah ibn Ubayy was the chief of the hypocrites, eloquent, large-bodied and handsome, and he used to attend the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ); when he spoke, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen to his speech.

Al-Kalbi said: the intended ones are Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Mu'attib ibn Qays, who had bodies, appearance and eloquence. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was said that it is to everyone who is suited to it. This is supported by the reading of whoever read yusma' ("be heard") in the passive.

It may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject. They were likened, in their sitting in the assemblies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaning against them, to propped-up timbers set against a wall, which neither understand nor know. They are like that, because they are empty of beneficial understanding and of knowledge by which its possessor benefits. Al-Zajjaj said: He described them with the perfection of their forms, then informed that in their lack of understanding and insight they are like timbers.

The majority read khushub ("timbers") with two ḍammahs; Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qunbul read it with the shin sukūn (khushb); and al-Bara' ibn Azib also read it so. Abu Ubayd preferred this, because its singular is khashabah, like badanah and budun. Abu Hatim preferred the first reading.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read it with two fatḥahs. The meaning of ﴿propped up﴾ (musannadah) is that they are leaned against something else, from the saying "I propped such-and-such against such-and-such"; the doubling of the letter is for intensification.

The first is that it is ʿalayhim ("against them"), and then His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining that they are the complete enemies, since they show what is contrary to what they conceal. The second possibility is that the second object of the verb of thinking is His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾, and ʿalayhim is then connected to ṣayḥah ("cry"). The plural pronoun came in accordance with the predicate, whereas the correct form would have been "he is the enemy". The first possibility is preferable.

Muqatil and al-Suddi said: meaning, when a caller calls out in the army, or an animal escapes, or a lost animal is announced, they think they are the ones meant, because of the terror in their hearts. From this is the verse of the poet:

It was also said: the hypocrites were in dread lest something be revealed concerning them which would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

Then Allah, the Glorified, commanded His Messenger to take his caution against them, saying: ﴿So beware of them﴾, lest they gain an opportunity against you or discover some of your secrets, for they are spies for your enemies among the disbelievers.

Then He invoked against them with His saying: ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they turned away?﴾, meaning: may Allah curse them. The Arabs sometimes use this expression in the manner of wonder, as in their saying "Allah fight him, what a poet!" or "How much he knows poetry!" This is not intended here; rather the intent is to censure and rebuke them. It is either a request made by Allah, the Glorified, of Himself, that He curse them and disgrace them, or it is teaching the believers to say it. Qatadah said: its meaning is "they deviate from the truth."

Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "they are turned away from right guidance."

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,"﴾ meaning: when a believer says to them, "Verses of the Qur'an have been revealed concerning you, so repent to Allah and His Messenger, and come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," ﴿they turn their heads﴾, meaning: they shake them in mockery at that.

Muqatil said: they twist their heads out of aversion to asking forgiveness.

The majority read lawwaw ("they twisted") with shaddah; Nafi' read it with the lightened form. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the first reading. ﴿And you see them turning away﴾, meaning: they turn away from the speech of whoever says to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," or they turn away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The clause ﴿while they are arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of the first circumstantial clause, which is "turning away"; because the seeing is visual, "turning away" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: you see them turning away and arrogant.

﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾, meaning: as long as they remain in hypocrisy. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, meaning: those who are complete in going out of obedience and immersed in the disobedience of Allah; the hypocrites enter this category by a stronger right.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned some of their ugly deeds, saying: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,"﴾ meaning: until they scatter away from him. By this they mean the poor among the Emigrants. The clause is resumptive, serving as the reason for their defiance, or for Allah's not forgiving them.

It is said: nafaḍa al-rajul waʿāʾahu min al-zād, fa-nfaḍḍa ("the man shook out his container of provisions, and it was emptied").

Then He, the Glorified, informed of the vastness of His dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the Provider of these Emigrants, because the treasuries of provision belong to Him; He gives whom He wills what He wills and withholds from whom He wills what He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, and do not know that the treasuries of sustenance are in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the Bestower and the Withholder, the Expander and the Restrainer.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned a hideous saying they uttered, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The one who uttered this saying was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites. By "the mightier" he meant himself and those with him, and by "the meaner" the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him. By "returning" he meant their return from that military expedition. The saying was attributed to the hypocrites, though the speaker was one individual among them, namely Abdullah ibn Ubayy, because he was their leader and the one in charge of their affairs, and they approved of what he said and obeyed him.

Then Allah, the Glorified, replied to the speaker of that saying, saying: ﴿But to Allah belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: strength and dominance belong to Allah alone, and to whoever He bestows it upon from among His messengers and righteous servants, not to anyone else.

O Allah, just as You have made might belong to the believers over the hypocrites, make might belong to the just among Your servants, and send humiliation upon the oppressive tyrants.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ what is beneficial so that they may do it, and what is harmful so that they may avoid it; rather they are like cattle, because of their extreme ignorance, their great bewilderment, and the sealing upon their hearts.

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the people were afflicted with hardship. Then they said: 'Zayd has lied against the Messenger of Allah.' So I felt a distress in myself at what they had said, until Allah revealed my confirmation in ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾. He said: "They were men of handsome appearance."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Allah named them hypocrites only because they concealed shirk (associating partners with Allah) and displayed faith."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾, that he said: "Their swearing by Allah that they are surely of you was a shield by which they protected themselves with their oaths from being killed and from war."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, that he said: "Standing palm trees."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah also narrated from him that he said: "This verse was revealed, ﴿They are the ones who say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,'﴾ concerning a hired laborer of Umar ibn al-Khattab."

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a military campaign — Sufyan said: 'They think it was the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq' — and a man from the Muhajirun (emigrants) struck (kasa'a) a man from the Ansar (helpers) on the buttocks. They said: 'A man from the Muhajirun struck a man from the Ansar.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave it, for it is foul.' Abdullah ibn Ubayy heard that and said: 'Have they really done this? By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and Umar stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions.'" Al-Tirmidhi added: "His son, Abdullah, said to him: 'By Allah, you will not return until you acknowledge that you are the lowly one, and the Messenger of Allah is the mighty one.' So he did."

Then He, the Glorified, informed of the vastness of His dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the Provider of these Emigrants, because the treasuries of provision belong to Him; He gives whom He wills what He wills and withholds from whom He wills what He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, and do not know that the treasuries of sustenance are in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the Bestower and the Withholder, the Expander and the Restrainer.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned a hideous saying they uttered, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The one who uttered this saying was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites. The saying was attributed to the hypocrites, though the speaker was one individual among them, namely Abdullah ibn Ubayy, because he was their leader and the one in charge of their affairs, and they approved of what he said and obeyed him.

Then Allah, the Glorified, replied to the speaker of that saying, saying: ﴿But to Allah belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: strength and dominance belong to Allah alone, and to whoever He bestows it upon from among His messengers and righteous servants, not to anyone else.

O Allah, just as You have made might belong to the believers over the hypocrites, make might belong to the just among Your servants, and send humiliation upon the oppressive tyrants.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ what is beneficial so that they may do it, and what is harmful so that they may avoid it; rather they are like cattle, because of their extreme ignorance, their great bewilderment, and the sealing upon their hearts.

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the people were afflicted with hardship. It was also said: the hypocrites were in dread lest something be revealed concerning them which would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

The majority read khushub ("timbers") with two ḍammahs; Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qunbul read it with the shin sukūn (khushb); and al-Bara' ibn Azib also read it so. Abu Ubayd preferred this, because its singular is khashabah, like badanah and budun. Abu Hatim preferred the first reading.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read it with two fatḥahs. The meaning of ﴿propped up﴾ (musannadah) is that they are leaned against something else, from the saying "I propped such-and-such against such-and-such"; the doubling of the letter is for intensification.

Then Allah, the Glorified, reproached them for cowardice, saying: ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, meaning: they think every shout they hear is aimed at them, falling upon them, because of their extreme cowardice and the terror in their hearts. The second object of the verb of thinking has two possibilities. It was also said: the hypocrites were in dread lest something be revealed concerning them which would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related, and al-Suyuti said with a hasan (good) chain, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite Surat al-Jumu'ah (the Chapter of Friday) in the Friday (Jumu'ah) prayer, which stirred up the believers, and in the second rak'ah Surat al-Munafiqun, by which he reproached the hypocrites."

Al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani related a similar report, raised to the Prophet, from Abu Inabah al-Khawlani.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, meaning: when they reach you and attend your assembly. The answer to the conditional is ﴿they say﴾. It was also said that the answer is omitted, and ﴿they say﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the sense is: they came to you saying such and such, so do not accept from them. It was also said that the answer is ﴿they have made their oaths a shield﴾, but this is far-fetched. ﴿They say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah."﴾ They emphasised their testimony with inna (indeed) and the lām (emphatic lām), to indicate that it issued from the depths of their hearts with sincere conviction. By "the hypocrites" is meant Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. The meaning of "we bear witness" is "we swear", so it functions as an oath, and for this reason it is followed by what follows an oath. From this is the verse of Qays ibn Dhurayh:

"I call Allah to witness that I love her; so this is her due from me, but what is her due from me is nothing [but love]."

Similar is "we know", for it too functions as an oath, as in the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I know that my appointed death will surely come; the arrows of death do not miss their mark."

The clause ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾ is a parenthetical clause, confirming what precedes it, namely what they displayed of testimony, even though their inner selves were contrary to that. ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, meaning: in their testimony, which they claimed came from the depths of the heart and sincere conviction, not in the literal content of their words, which is the testimony to the prophethood, for that is true.

The meaning is: Allah bears witness that they are liars in what their words contained of emphasis indicating that their testimony issued from sincere conviction, inner tranquillity and an inner state matching the outer one.

﴿They have made their oaths a shield﴾, meaning: they made the oaths with which they swore to you, that they are indeed of you, and that Muhammad is indeed the Messenger of Allah, a protection by which they guard themselves from you and a covering behind which they hide from being killed or taken captive. This clause is resumptive, explaining their lying and their swearing to it. The view of those who said it is the answer to the conditional has already been mentioned.

The majority read aymānahum with a fatḥah on the hamzah (aymānahum: "their oaths"); al-Hasan read it with a kasrah, and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Mujadilah.

﴿So they barred [others] from the way of Allah﴾, meaning: they prevented people from faith, from jihad and from acts of obedience, by means of what they produced of doubt and disparagement regarding prophethood. This is the meaning of ṣadd in the sense of "turning away". It may also be from ṣudūd (turning away), meaning: they turned away from entering the way of Allah and establishing His commands. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, namely of hypocrisy and barring.

In sā'a (evil is) there is the sense of wonder. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the lying, the barring and the ugliness of their deeds. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿because they believed﴾, meaning: because they believed outwardly out of hypocrisy and then disbelieved inwardly; or they showed belief to the believers and showed disbelief to the disbelievers. This is explicit in the disbelief of the hypocrites. It was also said that the verse was revealed about a people who believed and then apostatised. The first is preferable, as the context indicates.

﴿So a seal was set upon their hearts﴾, meaning: it was sealed over them because of their disbelief.

The majority read fa-ṭubi'a ("so it was sealed") in the passive, with the prepositional phrase after it serving as the deputy of the subject. Zayd ibn Ali read it in the active, with the subject a pronoun referring to Allah, the Glorified. This is supported by the reading of al-A'mash: "fa-ṭaba'a Allāhu 'alā qulūbihim" ("so Allah sealed their hearts"). ﴿So they do not understand﴾ what is in it of their welfare and guidance, which is faith.

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you﴾, meaning: their forms and appearances. The sense is that they have bodies which please whoever sees them, because of their freshness and splendour. ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, so you deem their words true and sincere, because of their eloquence and fluency of tongue. Abdullah ibn Ubayy was the chief of the hypocrites, eloquent, large-bodied and handsome, and he used to attend the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ); when he spoke, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen to his speech.

Al-Kalbi said: the intended ones are Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Mu'attib ibn Qays, who had bodies, appearance and eloquence. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was said that it is to everyone who is suited to it. This is supported by the reading of whoever read yusma' ("be heard") in the passive.

The clause ﴿as if they were propped-up timbers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what came before, that their bodies please the beholder and gladden the viewer. It may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject. They were likened, in their sitting in the assemblies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaning against them, to propped-up timbers set against a wall, which neither understand nor know. They are like that, because they are empty of beneficial understanding and of knowledge by which its possessor benefits. Al-Zajjaj said: He described them with the perfection of their forms, then informed that in their lack of understanding and insight they are like timbers.

The majority read khushub ("timbers") with two ḍammahs; Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qunbul read it with the shin sukūn (khushb); and al-Bara' ibn Azib also read it so. Abu Ubayd preferred this, because its singular is khashabah, like badanah and budun. Abu Hatim preferred the first reading.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read it with two fatḥahs. The meaning of ﴿propped up﴾ (musannadah) is that they are leaned against something else, from the saying "I propped such-and-such against such-and-such"; the doubling of the letter is for intensification.

Then Allah, the Glorified, reproached them for cowardice, saying: ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, meaning: they think every shout they hear is aimed at them, falling upon them, because of their extreme cowardice and the terror in their hearts. The second object of the verb of thinking has two possibilities. The first is that it is ʿalayhim ("against them"), and then His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining that they are the complete enemies, since they show what is contrary to what they conceal. The second possibility is that the second object of the verb of thinking is His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾, and ʿalayhim is then connected to ṣayḥah ("cry"). The plural pronoun came in accordance with the predicate, whereas the correct form would have been "he is the enemy". The first possibility is preferable.

Muqatil and al-Suddi said: meaning, when a caller calls out in the army, or an animal escapes, or a lost animal is announced, they think they are the ones meant, because of the terror in their hearts. From this is the verse of the poet:

"You keep thinking every thing after them is horsemen charging against them and men [attacking them]."

It was also said: the hypocrites were in dread lest something be revealed concerning them which would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

Then Allah, the Glorified, commanded His Messenger to take his caution against them, saying: ﴿So beware of them﴾, lest they gain an opportunity against you or discover some of your secrets, for they are spies for your enemies among the disbelievers.

Then He invoked against them with His saying: ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they turned away?﴾, meaning: may Allah curse them. The Arabs sometimes use this expression in the manner of wonder, as in their saying "Allah fight him, what a poet!" or "How much he knows poetry!" This is not intended here; rather the intent is to censure and rebuke them. It is either a request made by Allah, the Glorified, of Himself, that He curse them and disgrace them, or it is teaching the believers to say it. The meaning of ﴿how are they turned away?﴾ is: how are they diverted from the truth and inclined away from it toward disbelief?

Qatadah said: its meaning is "they deviate from the truth."

Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "they are turned away from right guidance."

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,"﴾ meaning: when a believer says to them, "Verses of the Qur'an have been revealed concerning you, so repent to Allah and His Messenger, and come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," ﴿they turn their heads﴾, meaning: they shake them in mockery at that.

Muqatil said: they twist their heads out of aversion to asking forgiveness.

The majority read lawwaw ("they twisted") with shaddah; Nafi' read it with the lightened form. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the first reading. ﴿And you see them turning away﴾, meaning: they turn away from the speech of whoever says to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," or they turn away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The clause ﴿while they are arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of the first circumstantial clause, which is "turning away"; because the seeing is visual, "turning away" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: you see them turning away and arrogant.

﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, meaning: asking forgiveness and not asking are equal; it will not benefit them, because of their persistence in hypocrisy and their continuance in disbelief.

The majority read astaghfarta with a hamzah with fatḥah and without a madd, dropping the interrogative hamzah, relying on the indication of am ("or") that it is there. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read it with a hamzah then an alif.

﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾, meaning: as long as they remain in hypocrisy. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, meaning: those who are complete in going out of obedience and immersed in the disobedience of Allah; the hypocrites enter this category by a stronger right.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned some of their ugly deeds, saying: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,"﴾ meaning: until they scatter away from him. By this they mean the poor among the Emigrants. The clause is resumptive, serving as the reason for their defiance, or for Allah's not forgiving them.

The majority read yanfaḍḍū ("they disperse") from infiḍāḍ, which means dispersal. Al-Fadl ibn Isa al-Raqashi read yunfiḍū, from anfaḍa al-qawm, when their provisions run out. It is said: nafaḍa al-rajul waʿāʾahu min al-zād, fa-nfaḍḍa ("the man shook out his container of provisions, and it was emptied").

Then He, the Glorified, informed of the vastness of His dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the Provider of these Emigrants, because the treasuries of provision belong to Him; He gives whom He wills what He wills and withholds from whom He wills what He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, and do not know that the treasuries of sustenance are in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the Bestower and the Withholder, the Expander and the Restrainer.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned a hideous saying they uttered, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The one who uttered this saying was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites. By "the mightier" he meant himself and those with him, and by "the meaner" the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him. By "returning" he meant their return from that military expedition. The saying was attributed to the hypocrites, though the speaker was one individual among them, namely Abdullah ibn Ubayy, because he was their leader and the one in charge of their affairs, and they approved of what he said and obeyed him.

Then Allah, the Glorified, replied to the speaker of that saying, saying: ﴿But to Allah belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: strength and dominance belong to Allah alone, and to whoever He bestows it upon from among His messengers and righteous servants, not to anyone else.

O Allah, just as You have made might belong to the believers over the hypocrites, make might belong to the just among Your servants, and send humiliation upon the oppressive tyrants.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ what is beneficial so that they may do it, and what is harmful so that they may avoid it; rather they are like cattle, because of their extreme ignorance, their great bewilderment, and the sealing upon their hearts.

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the people were afflicted with hardship. Abdullah ibn Ubayy said to his companions: 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him,' and he said: 'If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and he sent for Abdullah ibn Ubayy and questioned him. He solemnly swore that he had not done it. Then they said: 'Zayd has lied against the Messenger of Allah.' So I felt a distress in myself at what they had said, until Allah revealed my confirmation in ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) then called them to ask forgiveness for them, but they turned their heads away, and this is His saying ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾." He said: "They were men of handsome appearance."

It was also narrated from him, in a longer form than this, by Ibn Sa'd, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Allah named them hypocrites only because they concealed shirk (associating partners with Allah) and displayed faith."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾, that he said: "Their swearing by Allah that they are surely of you was a shield by which they protected themselves with their oaths from being killed and from war."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, that he said: "Standing palm trees."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah also narrated from him that he said: "This verse was revealed, ﴿They are the ones who say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,'﴾ concerning a hired laborer of Umar ibn al-Khattab."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam and Ibn Mas'ud that they both recited: "Do not spend on those who are with (عِنْدِ) the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him."

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a military campaign — Sufyan said: 'They think it was the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq' — and a man from the Muhajirun (emigrants) struck (kasa'a) a man from the Ansar (helpers) on the buttocks. The Muhajiri said: 'O Muhajirun!' and the Ansari said: 'O Ansar!' The Prophet (ﷺ) heard that and said: 'What is this with the call of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance)?' They said: 'A man from the Muhajirun struck a man from the Ansar.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave it, for it is foul.' Abdullah ibn Ubayy heard that and said: 'Have they really done this? By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and Umar stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions.'" Al-Tirmidhi added: "His son, Abdullah, said to him: 'By Allah, you will not return until you acknowledge that you are the lowly one, and the Messenger of Allah is the mighty one.' So he did."

The Surah is Madaniyyah (revealed at Madinah).

Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Then He, the Glorified, informed of the vastness of His dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the Provider of these Emigrants, because the treasuries of provision belong to Him; He gives whom He wills what He wills and withholds from whom He wills what He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, and do not know that the treasuries of sustenance are in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the Bestower and the Withholder, the Expander and the Restrainer.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned a hideous saying they uttered, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The one who uttered this saying was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites. By "the mightier" he meant himself and those with him, and by "the meaner" the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him. By "returning" he meant their return from that military expedition. The saying was attributed to the hypocrites, though the speaker was one individual among them, namely Abdullah ibn Ubayy, because he was their leader and the one in charge of their affairs, and they approved of what he said and obeyed him.

Then Allah, the Glorified, replied to the speaker of that saying, saying: ﴿But to Allah belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: strength and dominance belong to Allah alone, and to whoever He bestows it upon from among His messengers and righteous servants, not to anyone else.

O Allah, just as You have made might belong to the believers over the hypocrites, make might belong to the just among Your servants, and send humiliation upon the oppressive tyrants.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ what is beneficial so that they may do it, and what is harmful so that they may avoid it; rather they are like cattle, because of their extreme ignorance, their great bewilderment, and the sealing upon their hearts.

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the people were afflicted with hardship. Abdullah ibn Ubayy said to his companions: 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him,' and he said: 'If we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and he sent for Abdullah ibn Ubayy and questioned him. He solemnly swore that he had not done it. Then they said: 'Zayd has lied against the Messenger of Allah.' So I felt a distress in myself at what they had said, until Allah revealed my confirmation in ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾. The Prophet (ﷺ) then called them to ask forgiveness for them, but they turned their heads away, and this is His saying ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾." He said: "They were men of handsome appearance."

It was also narrated from him, in a longer form than this, by Ibn Sa'd, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Allah named them hypocrites only because they concealed shirk (associating partners with Allah) and displayed faith."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him regarding ﴿They have taken their oaths as a shield﴾, that he said: "Their swearing by Allah that they are surely of you was a shield by which they protected themselves with their oaths from being killed and from war."

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, that he said: "Standing palm trees."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah also narrated from him that he said: "This verse was revealed, ﴿They are the ones who say, 'Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,'﴾ concerning a hired laborer of Umar ibn al-Khattab."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam and Ibn Mas'ud that they both recited: "Do not spend on those who are with (عِنْدِ) the Messenger of Allah until they disperse from around him."

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a military campaign — Sufyan said: 'They think it was the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq' — and a man from the Muhajirun (emigrants) struck (kasa'a) a man from the Ansar (helpers) on the buttocks. The Muhajiri said: 'O Muhajirun!' and the Ansari said: 'O Ansar!' The Prophet (ﷺ) heard that and said: 'What is this with the call of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period of ignorance)?' They said: 'A man from the Muhajirun struck a man from the Ansar.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave it, for it is foul.' Abdullah ibn Ubayy heard that and said: 'Have they really done this? By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and Umar stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions.'" Al-Tirmidhi added: "His son, Abdullah, said to him: 'By Allah, you will not return until you acknowledge that you are the lowly one, and the Messenger of Allah is the mighty one.' So he did."

The Surah is Madaniyyah (revealed at Madinah).

Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the consensus."

Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "Surat al-Munafiqun (the Chapter of the Hypocrites) was revealed at Madinah."

Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related, and al-Suyuti said with a hasan (good) chain, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite Surat al-Jumu'ah (the Chapter of Friday) in the Friday (Jumu'ah) prayer, which stirred up the believers, and in the second rak'ah Surat al-Munafiqun, by which he reproached the hypocrites."

Al-Bazzar and al-Tabarani related a similar report, raised to the Prophet, from Abu Inabah al-Khawlani.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying: ﴿When the hypocrites come to you﴾, meaning: when they reach you and attend your assembly. The answer to the conditional is ﴿they say﴾. It was also said that the answer is omitted, and ﴿they say﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), and the sense is: they came to you saying such and such, so do not accept from them. It was also said that the answer is ﴿they have made their oaths a shield﴾, but this is far-fetched. ﴿They say, "We bear witness that you are indeed the Messenger of Allah."﴾ They emphasised their testimony with inna (indeed) and the lām (emphatic lām), to indicate that it issued from the depths of their hearts with sincere conviction. By "the hypocrites" is meant Abdullah ibn Ubayy and his companions. The meaning of "we bear witness" is "we swear", so it functions as an oath, and for this reason it is followed by what follows an oath. From this is the verse of Qays ibn Dhurayh:

"I call Allah to witness that I love her; so this is her due from me, but what is her due from me is nothing [but love]."

Similar is "we know", for it too functions as an oath, as in the verse of the poet:

"Indeed I know that my appointed death will surely come; the arrows of death do not miss their mark."

The clause ﴿And Allah knows that you are indeed His Messenger﴾ is a parenthetical clause, confirming what precedes it, namely what they displayed of testimony, even though their inner selves were contrary to that. ﴿And Allah bears witness that the hypocrites are indeed liars﴾, meaning: in their testimony, which they claimed came from the depths of the heart and sincere conviction, not in the literal content of their words, which is the testimony to the prophethood, for that is true.

The meaning is: Allah bears witness that they are liars in what their words contained of emphasis indicating that their testimony issued from sincere conviction, inner tranquillity and an inner state matching the outer one.

﴿They have made their oaths a shield﴾, meaning: they made the oaths with which they swore to you, that they are indeed of you, and that Muhammad is indeed the Messenger of Allah, a protection by which they guard themselves from you and a covering behind which they hide from being killed or taken captive. This clause is resumptive, explaining their lying and their swearing to it. The view of those who said it is the answer to the conditional has already been mentioned.

The majority read aymānahum with a fatḥah on the hamzah (aymānahum: "their oaths"); al-Hasan read it with a kasrah, and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Mujadilah.

﴿So they barred [others] from the way of Allah﴾, meaning: they prevented people from faith, from jihad and from acts of obedience, by means of what they produced of doubt and disparagement regarding prophethood. This is the meaning of ṣadd in the sense of "turning away". It may also be from ṣudūd (turning away), meaning: they turned away from entering the way of Allah and establishing His commands. ﴿Indeed, evil is what they used to do﴾, namely of hypocrisy and barring.

In sā'a (evil is) there is the sense of wonder. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers to what was mentioned before: the lying, the barring and the ugliness of their deeds. It is the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is ﴿because they believed﴾, meaning: because they believed outwardly out of hypocrisy and then disbelieved inwardly; or they showed belief to the believers and showed disbelief to the disbelievers. This is explicit in the disbelief of the hypocrites. It was also said that the verse was revealed about a people who believed and then apostatised. The first is preferable, as the context indicates.

﴿So a seal was set upon their hearts﴾, meaning: it was sealed over them because of their disbelief.

The majority read fa-ṭubi'a ("so it was sealed") in the passive, with the prepositional phrase after it serving as the deputy of the subject. Zayd ibn Ali read it in the active, with the subject a pronoun referring to Allah, the Glorified. This is supported by the reading of al-A'mash: "fa-ṭaba'a Allāhu 'alā qulūbihim" ("so Allah sealed their hearts"). ﴿So they do not understand﴾ what is in it of their welfare and guidance, which is faith.

﴿And when you see them, their bodies please you﴾, meaning: their forms and appearances. The sense is that they have bodies which please whoever sees them, because of their freshness and splendour. ﴿And if they speak, you listen to their speech﴾, so you deem their words true and sincere, because of their eloquence and fluency of tongue. Abdullah ibn Ubayy was the chief of the hypocrites, eloquent, large-bodied and handsome, and he used to attend the assembly of the Prophet (ﷺ); when he spoke, the Prophet (ﷺ) would listen to his speech.

Al-Kalbi said: the intended ones are Abdullah ibn Ubayy, Jadd ibn Qays and Mu'attib ibn Qays, who had bodies, appearance and eloquence. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it was said that it is to everyone who is suited to it. This is supported by the reading of whoever read yusma' ("be heard") in the passive.

The clause ﴿as if they were propped-up timbers﴾ is a resumptive clause, confirming what came before, that their bodies please the beholder and gladden the viewer. It may also be in the nominative position, as the predicate of an omitted subject. They were likened, in their sitting in the assemblies of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaning against them, to propped-up timbers set against a wall, which neither understand nor know. They are like that, because they are empty of beneficial understanding and of knowledge by which its possessor benefits. Al-Zajjaj said: He described them with the perfection of their forms, then informed that in their lack of understanding and insight they are like timbers.

The majority read khushub ("timbers") with two ḍammahs; Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Qunbul read it with the shin sukūn (khushb); and al-Bara' ibn Azib also read it so. Abu Ubayd preferred this, because its singular is khashabah, like badanah and budun. Abu Hatim preferred the first reading.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab read it with two fatḥahs. The meaning of ﴿propped up﴾ (musannadah) is that they are leaned against something else, from the saying "I propped such-and-such against such-and-such"; the doubling of the letter is for intensification.

Then Allah, the Glorified, reproached them for cowardice, saying: ﴿They think every cry is against them﴾, meaning: they think every shout they hear is aimed at them, falling upon them, because of their extreme cowardice and the terror in their hearts. The second object of the verb of thinking has two possibilities. The first is that it is ʿalayhim ("against them"), and then His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾ is a resumptive clause explaining that they are the complete enemies, since they show what is contrary to what they conceal. The second possibility is that the second object of the verb of thinking is His saying ﴿They are the enemy﴾, and ʿalayhim is then connected to ṣayḥah ("cry"). The plural pronoun came in accordance with the predicate, whereas the correct form would have been "he is the enemy". The first possibility is preferable.

Muqatil and al-Suddi said: meaning, when a caller calls out in the army, or an animal escapes, or a lost animal is announced, they think they are the ones meant, because of the terror in their hearts. From this is the verse of the poet:

"You keep thinking every thing after them is horsemen charging against them and men [attacking them]."

It was also said: the hypocrites were in dread lest something be revealed concerning them which would expose their concealments and make their blood and property lawful.

Then Allah, the Glorified, commanded His Messenger to take his caution against them, saying: ﴿So beware of them﴾, lest they gain an opportunity against you or discover some of your secrets, for they are spies for your enemies among the disbelievers.

Then He invoked against them with His saying: ﴿May Allah destroy them; how are they turned away?﴾, meaning: may Allah curse them. The Arabs sometimes use this expression in the manner of wonder, as in their saying "Allah fight him, what a poet!" or "How much he knows poetry!" This is not intended here; rather the intent is to censure and rebuke them. It is either a request made by Allah, the Glorified, of Himself, that He curse them and disgrace them, or it is teaching the believers to say it. The meaning of ﴿how are they turned away?﴾ is: how are they diverted from the truth and inclined away from it toward disbelief?

Qatadah said: its meaning is "they deviate from the truth."

Al-Hasan said: its meaning is "they are turned away from right guidance."

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you,"﴾ meaning: when a believer says to them, "Verses of the Qur'an have been revealed concerning you, so repent to Allah and His Messenger, and come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," ﴿they turn their heads﴾, meaning: they shake them in mockery at that.

Muqatil said: they twist their heads out of aversion to asking forgiveness.

The majority read lawwaw ("they twisted") with shaddah; Nafi' read it with the lightened form. Abu 'Ubayd preferred the first reading. ﴿And you see them turning away﴾, meaning: they turn away from the speech of whoever says to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," or they turn away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The clause ﴿while they are arrogant﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause from the subject of the first circumstantial clause, which is "turning away"; because the seeing is visual, "turning away" is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. The meaning is: you see them turning away and arrogant.

﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾, meaning: asking forgiveness and not asking are equal; it will not benefit them, because of their persistence in hypocrisy and their continuance in disbelief.

The majority read astaghfarta with a hamzah with fatḥah and without a madd, dropping the interrogative hamzah, relying on the indication of am ("or") that it is there. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read it with a hamzah then an alif.

﴿Allah will never forgive them﴾, meaning: as long as they remain in hypocrisy. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the defiant people﴾, meaning: those who are complete in going out of obedience and immersed in the disobedience of Allah; the hypocrites enter this category by a stronger right.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned some of their ugly deeds, saying: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of Allah until they disperse,"﴾ meaning: until they scatter away from him. By this they mean the poor among the Emigrants. The clause is resumptive, serving as the reason for their defiance, or for Allah's not forgiving them.

The majority read yanfaḍḍū ("they disperse") from infiḍāḍ, which means dispersal. Al-Fadl ibn Isa al-Raqashi read yunfiḍū, from anfaḍa al-qawm, when their provisions run out. It is said: nafaḍa al-rajul waʿāʾahu min al-zād, fa-nfaḍḍa ("the man shook out his container of provisions, and it was emptied").

Then He, the Glorified, informed of the vastness of His dominion, saying: ﴿To Allah belong the treasuries of the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning: He is the Provider of these Emigrants, because the treasuries of provision belong to Him; He gives whom He wills what He wills and withholds from whom He wills what He wills. ﴿But the hypocrites do not understand﴾ this, and do not know that the treasuries of sustenance are in the hand of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that He is the Bestower and the Withholder, the Expander and the Restrainer.

Then He, the Glorified, mentioned a hideous saying they uttered, saying: ﴿They say, "If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it."﴾ The one who uttered this saying was Abdullah ibn Ubayy, chief of the hypocrites. By "the mightier" he meant himself and those with him, and by "the meaner" the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him. By "returning" he meant their return from that military expedition. The saying was attributed to the hypocrites, though the speaker was one individual among them, namely Abdullah ibn Ubayy, because he was their leader and the one in charge of their affairs, and they approved of what he said and obeyed him.

Then Allah, the Glorified, replied to the speaker of that saying, saying: ﴿But to Allah belongs the might, and to His Messenger, and to the believers﴾, meaning: strength and dominance belong to Allah alone, and to whoever He bestows it upon from among His messengers and righteous servants, not to anyone else.

O Allah, just as You have made might belong to the believers over the hypocrites, make might belong to the just among Your servants, and send humiliation upon the oppressive tyrants.

﴿But the hypocrites do not know﴾ what is beneficial so that they may do it, and what is harmful so that they may avoid it; rather they are like cattle, because of their extreme ignorance, their great bewilderment, and the sealing upon their hearts.

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on a journey, and the people were afflicted with hardship. I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and informed him of that, and he sent for Abdullah ibn Ubayy and questioned him. He solemnly swore that he had not done it. The Prophet (ﷺ) then called them to ask forgiveness for them, but they turned their heads away, and this is His saying ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾." He said: "They were men of handsome appearance."

It was also narrated from him, in a longer form than this, by Ibn Sa'd, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sahih), Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who graded it sahih), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi.

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, regarding ﴿as if they were propped-up pieces of wood﴾, that he said: "Standing palm trees."

And al-Bukhari, Muslim, and others narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "We were with the Prophet (ﷺ) in a military campaign — Sufyan said: 'They think it was the campaign of Banu al-Mustaliq' — and a man from the Muhajirun (emigrants) struck (kasa'a) a man from the Ansar (helpers) on the buttocks. By Allah, if we return to Medina, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and Umar stood up and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, let me strike the neck of this hypocrite.' The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'Leave him, so that people do not say that Muhammad kills his companions.'" Al-Tirmidhi added: "His son, Abdullah, said to him: 'By Allah, you will not return until you acknowledge that you are the lowly one, and the Messenger of Allah is the mighty one.' So he did."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 63, verse 9–11:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the vices of the hypocrites, He returned to addressing the believers, encouraging them to remember Him, so He said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah.﴾ He thereby warned them against the character of the hypocrites, whose wealth and children had diverted them from the remembrance of Allah. The meaning of ﴿let not... divert you﴾ is: let not... occupy you. By "the remembrance" is meant the obligations of Islam (farā'id al-Islām), as stated by al-Hasan.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the five daily prayers. It was also said: it means the recitation of the Qur'an. And it was said: this is an address to the hypocrites, and their being described as believers is because they had outwardly believed. The first view is preferable. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ — that is, whoever becomes absorbed in this world away from the religion — ﴿those are the losers﴾, that is, the complete losers.

﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾. The apparent meaning is that the intended spending is spending in good causes in its general sense, and "min" (from) is partitive, meaning: spend part of what We have provided you in the way of good. It was also said: the intended meaning is the obligatory zakat, before death comes to one of you, by its signs descending upon him and his witnessing the presence of its indicators. The object is placed before the verb for emphasis. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term"﴾, that is, he says at the arrival of what has descended upon him, calling out to his Lord: "Why not grant me respite and delay my death to a near term," that is, a short duration. ﴿And I would give charity﴾, that is, I would give charity from my wealth. ﴿And be among the righteous.﴾ The majority read ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾ with the assimilation of the tā' into the ṣād, and it is in the accusative as the answer to the wish (jawāb al-tamannī). It was also said that the "lā" in "lawlā" is extra, and the original is "law akhkhartanī" (if only You had delayed me).

Abū ʿAmr... [note: the following reading is recorded as: ] Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read ﴿fa-ataṣaddaq﴾ without assimilation, according to the original form.

The majority read ﴿wa-akun﴾ with jazm (jussive), on the position of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾, as if it were said: if You delay me, I will give charity and be [among the righteous]. Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is "lawlā akhkhartanī" (why not delay me). The jussive of "akun" is on the position of "fa-aṣṣaddaq," since it carries the sense: if You delay me, I will give charity and I will be.

So said Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and others.

Sībawayh, quoting al-Khalīl, said: it is jussive by the implied conditional which the wish indicates, and Sībawayh made this similar to the verse of Zuhayr:

*Badā lī annī lastu mudrika mā maḍā / wa-lā sābiqan shay'an idhā kāna jā'iyan*
It has become clear to me that I cannot overtake what has passed, nor outrun anything that is coming.

Here "wa-lā sābiqan" is in the genitive, coordinated with "mudrik," which is the predicate of "laysa," on the supposition of an extra "bā'" in it.

Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Mujāhid read ﴿wa-akūna﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾, and its basis is clear.

However, Abū ʿUbayd said: I saw in the Muṣḥaf of ʿUthmān ﴿wa-akun﴾ without a wāw. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿wa-akūnu﴾ in the nominative, as a new sentence, meaning: "and I will be."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: death does not come upon anyone who has not performed the Ḥajj nor paid zakat except that he asks for a return, and he recited this verse.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered this one who wishes, saying: ﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come.﴾ That is, when its term has arrived and its lifespan has ended. ﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

The majority read ﴿ta'malūn﴾ with the second person (ta), addressing them; Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim and al-Sulamī read it with the third person (ya), as a report.

It has been reported that Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding His saying ﴿O you who have believed, let not...﴾, the verse, that he said: "They are servants from my community, the righteous among them; neither trade nor sale diverts them from the remembrance of Allah, nor from the five obligatory prayers."

ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Whoever has wealth that enables him to reach the House of Allah (for Ḥajj), or upon which zakat is due, and does not do it, will ask for a return at death." A man said: "O Ibn ʿAbbās, fear Allah, for only the disbeliever asks for a return!" So he said: "I will recite to you a Qur'an about that: ﴿O you who have believed...﴾ to the end of the surah."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 63, verse 9–11:

When Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the vices of the hypocrites, He returned to addressing the believers, encouraging them to remember Him, so He said: ﴿O you who have believed, let not your wealth or your children divert you from the remembrance of Allah.﴾ He thereby warned them against the character of the hypocrites, whose wealth and children had diverted them from the remembrance of Allah. The meaning of ﴿let not... divert you﴾ is: let not... occupy you. By "the remembrance" is meant the obligations of Islam (farā'id al-Islām), as stated by al-Hasan.

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: it means the five daily prayers. It was also said: it means the recitation of the Qur'an. And it was said: this is an address to the hypocrites, and their being described as believers is because they had outwardly believed. The first view is preferable. ﴿And whoever does that﴾ — that is, whoever becomes absorbed in this world away from the religion — ﴿those are the losers﴾, that is, the complete losers.

﴿And spend from what We have provided you﴾. The apparent meaning is that the intended spending is spending in good causes in its general sense, and "min" (from) is partitive, meaning: spend part of what We have provided you in the way of good. It was also said: the intended meaning is the obligatory zakat, before death comes to one of you, by its signs descending upon him and his witnessing the presence of its indicators. The object is placed before the verb for emphasis. ﴿Then he says, "My Lord, if only You would delay me to a near term"﴾, that is, he says at the arrival of what has descended upon him, calling out to his Lord: "Why not grant me respite and delay my death to a near term," that is, a short duration. ﴿And I would give charity﴾, that is, I would give charity from my wealth. ﴿And be among the righteous.﴾ The majority read ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾ with the assimilation of the tā' into the ṣād, and it is in the accusative as the answer to the wish (jawāb al-tamannī). It was also said that the "lā" in "lawlā" is extra, and the original is "law akhkhartanī" (if only You had delayed me).

Abū ʿAmr... [note: the following reading is recorded as: ] Ubayy and Ibn Masʿūd, and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr read ﴿fa-ataṣaddaq﴾ without assimilation, according to the original form.

The majority read ﴿wa-akun﴾ with jazm (jussive), on the position of ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾, as if it were said: if You delay me, I will give charity and be [among the righteous]. Al-Zajjāj said: its meaning is "lawlā akhkhartanī" (why not delay me). The jussive of "akun" is on the position of "fa-aṣṣaddaq," since it carries the sense: if You delay me, I will give charity and I will be.

So said Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, and others.

Sībawayh, quoting al-Khalīl, said: it is jussive by the implied conditional which the wish indicates, and Sībawayh made this similar to the verse of Zuhayr:

*Badā lī annī lastu mudrika mā maḍā / wa-lā sābiqan shay'an idhā kāna jā'iyan*
It has become clear to me that I cannot overtake what has passed, nor outrun anything that is coming.

Here "wa-lā sābiqan" is in the genitive, coordinated with "mudrik," which is the predicate of "laysa," on the supposition of an extra "bā'" in it.

Abū ʿAmr, Ibn Muḥaysin, and Mujāhid read ﴿wa-akūna﴾ in the accusative, coordinated with ﴿fa-aṣṣaddaq﴾, and its basis is clear.

However, Abū ʿUbayd said: I saw in the Muṣḥaf of ʿUthmān ﴿wa-akun﴾ without a wāw. ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr read ﴿wa-akūnu﴾ in the nominative, as a new sentence, meaning: "and I will be."

Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: death does not come upon anyone who has not performed the Ḥajj nor paid zakat except that he asks for a return, and he recited this verse.

Then Allah, glorified is He, answered this one who wishes, saying: ﴿And Allah will never delay a soul when its term has come.﴾ That is, when its term has arrived and its lifespan has ended. ﴿And Allah is All-Aware of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Him, so He will recompense you for your deeds.

The majority read ﴿ta'malūn﴾ with the second person (ta), addressing them; Abū Bakr on the authority of ʿĀṣim and al-Sulamī read it with the third person (ya), as a report.
